title: AI Agent Drift: How to Detect Behavior Changes in Production
summary: Detect AI agent drift in production: compare recent runs with a baseline on run shape, tool mix and failure share, then attribute shifts to releases or traffic.
body_markdown:
AI agent drift is a change in an agent's behavior across runs compared with its recent baseline. A prompt edit ships, tool calls climb, and individual traces still look plausible. To decide whether you're seeing a regression, compare recent runs with a baseline, then separate release effects from traffic changes.


Laminar has no native statistical anomaly detection. This guide uses SQL you schedule and own, alongside Signal findings. The worked example is a simulated project with seeded behavior changes and Issues findings, not a test of evaluator accuracy.


*A simulated research agent one day after a release: tool calls per run crossed the example threshold while the error rate fell and the seeded Issues share stayed below its threshold.*


## What agent drift looks like: a simulated regression#


The project contains 6,537 synthetic traces over two weeks from two agents: one planted regression and one traffic change. Issues findings were seeded, not model-evaluated. The effect sizes are constructed; the query results were measured against that synthetic data.


The research agent searches the web, fetches pages, reads PDFs and writes a report. Release 7d2f41b


represents a truncated-page bug: three to five extra consecutive fetch_page


calls in 38% of its runs, with a 13-point higher chance of an Issues finding on those runs.


The comparison uses a 24-hour window ending 1 hour ago and the preceding 7 days, about one day after full rollout:


Research agent Baseline (7 days) Recent 24 hours


Runs 366 per day 441


Tool calls per run 6.55 8.10


p90 tokens per run 68,811 119,837


p90 duration 40.6 s 55.3 s


Runs with an error span 2.5% 1.1%


Analyzed runs with an Issues finding 6.7% 9.8%


An error-rate alert sees an improvement. The Issues share exceeded the 3.9% to 7.5% daily range through November 17, but its z-score was 2.3, below this guide's example outcome threshold of 3. Tool calls per run moved by 14 standard errors and crossed the example threshold of 4 within ten hours of full rollout.


That ordering follows from the scenario's construction: affected runs received extra calls, while findings appeared on only a fraction of them. Watch behavior and outcomes together, and check which moves first on your traffic.


## Four kinds of agent drift#


Drift type What changes How you measure it


Input or task mix What users ask for Share of runs per segment


Run shape Steps, tool calls, tokens, latency, errors Per-run averages and percentiles


Behavior mix Which tools run, how often one repeats Tool share, repeated-call rate


Outcome Detected failures Share of analyzed runs with a finding, new clusters


Input drift isn't a regression by itself, but it can move the other three layers. Attribution matters before you act.


Per-trace failure detection, covered in[Automatic Failure Detection for AI Agents](https://laminar.sh/article/ai-agent-failure-detection) , evaluates individual runs. Drift detection compares populations. One run with nine tool calls needn't be a failure; a thousand such runs after a deploy can warrant investigation.


## Compare a recent window against a baseline#


Compare the same per-run metrics in both windows. Laminar's[SQL editor](https://laminar.sh/docs/platform/sql-editor) exposes spans, traces and Signal results together, so one query can return run shape and outcome findings:


```text
WITH   runs   AS     (
SELECT
trace_id  ,
anyIf  (  name  ,   parent_span_id   =   toUUID  (  '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000'  )  )     AS   agent  ,
min  (  start_time  )     >=     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     25     HOUR     AS   recent  ,
countIf  (  span_type   =     'TOOL'  )     AS   tool_calls  ,
sum  (  total_tokens  )     AS   tokens  ,
trace_id   IN     (
SELECT   trace_id   FROM   signal_runs
WHERE   signal_id   IN     (  SELECT   id   FROM   signals   WHERE   name   =     'Issues'  )
AND     status     =     'COMPLETED'
AND   updated_at   >=     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     9     DAY
)     AS   analyzed  ,
trace_id   IN     (
SELECT   trace_id   FROM   signal_events
WHERE   signal_name   =     'Issues'
AND   severity   >=     1
AND     timestamp     >=     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     9     DAY
)     AS   flagged
FROM   spans
WHERE   start_time   >=     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     193     HOUR
AND   trace_id   IN     (
SELECT   id   FROM   traces
WHERE   start_time   >=     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     193     HOUR
AND   start_time   <     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     1     HOUR
)
GROUP     BY   trace_id
)
SELECT
agent  ,
countIf  (  NOT   recent  )     AS   baseline_runs  ,
countIf  (  recent  )     AS   recent_runs  ,
round  (  avgIf  (  tool_calls  ,     NOT   recent  )  ,     2  )     AS   baseline_tools  ,
round  (  avgIf  (  tool_calls  ,   recent  )  ,     2  )     AS   recent_tools  ,
round  (  (  recent_tools   -   baseline_tools  )
/   sqrt  (  varSampIf  (  tool_calls  ,     NOT   recent  )     /   baseline_runs
+   varSampIf  (  tool_calls  ,   recent  )     /   recent_runs  )  ,     1  )     AS   tools_z  ,
round  (  avgIf  (  tokens  ,   recent  )     /   avgIf  (  tokens  ,     NOT   recent  )     -     1  ,     2  )     AS   tokens_change  ,
countIf  (  analyzed   AND     NOT   recent  )     AS   baseline_analyzed  ,
countIf  (  analyzed   AND   recent  )     AS   recent_analyzed  ,
round  (  baseline_analyzed   /   baseline_runs  ,     2  )     AS   baseline_coverage  ,
round  (  recent_analyzed   /   recent_runs  ,     2  )     AS   recent_coverage  ,
round  (  countIf  (  flagged   AND   analyzed   AND     NOT   recent  )     /   baseline_analyzed  ,     3  )     AS   baseline_flagged  ,
round  (  countIf  (  flagged   AND   analyzed   AND   recent  )     /   recent_analyzed  ,     3  )     AS   recent_flagged  ,
round  (  countIf  (  flagged   AND   analyzed  )     /   countIf  (  analyzed  )  ,     4  )     AS   pooled_flagged  ,
if  (  baseline_analyzed   >=     200     AND   recent_analyzed   >=     100     AND   pooled_flagged   *   recent_analyzed   >=     5  ,
round  (  (  recent_flagged   -   baseline_flagged  )
/   sqrt  (  pooled_flagged   *     (  1     -   pooled_flagged  )
*     (  1     /   baseline_analyzed   +     1     /   recent_analyzed  )  )  ,     1  )  ,
NULL  )     AS   flagged_z
FROM   runs
WHERE   agent   !=     ''
GROUP     BY   agent
HAVING   baseline_runs   >=     200     AND   recent_runs   >=     50
ORDER     BY   abs  (  tools_z  )     DESC


```


The query returned these selected columns:


agent recent_runs tools tools_z tokens coverage flagged share flagged_z


research_agent 441 6.55 → 8.10 14.1 +42% 1.00 → 1.00 0.067 → 0.098 2.3


ticket_triage 161 2.57 → 3.58 7.0 +123% 0.74 → 0.83 0.043 → 0.067 1.2


Treat the z-scores as screening statistics under an independence assumption, rather than calibrated anomaly tests. tools_z


divides the mean difference by its standard error. flagged_z


uses a pooled two-proportion calculation. A null


outcome statistic means the comparison is unavailable. It does not establish that nothing changed.


The query includes several safeguards:


- **Maturity lag.** The recent window ends an hour ago to reduce incomplete runs and evaluation lag. Increase it for longer runs or for batch-mode Signals, which return results within several hours.
- **Outcome cohort.** Issues defaults to traces with more than 1,000 tokens. Findings count only among runs with completed Issues analysis. Coverage rose from 74% to 83% for triage because the traffic change added longer tickets: eligibility moved, not just quality.
- **Volume guards.** The HAVING


clause drops agents with too few runs. The outcome calculation has additional minimums for analyzed runs and expected findings.


A backtest covered nine timestamps before either change, from November 14 to 17. Tool-call z-scores ranged from -1.7 to 1.2; the outcome z-score peaked at 2.4. At five of the nine timestamps, triage's flagged_z


was null


, with under 100 analyzed runs. Checks 4 and 10 hours into full rollout put the research agent's tools_z


at 2.9 and 7.7.


The thresholds of 4 and 3 are illustrative. Calibrate yours on your history, including weekly seasonality, which this simulation doesn't model. Name the top span consistently: this query treats that name as the agent's identity.


## Tool mix and repeated calls: behavior drift#


After run shape flags a change, compare each tool's share of calls:


```text
SELECT
name   AS   tool  ,
round  (  countIf  (  start_time   <     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     25     HOUR  )
/     sum  (  countIf  (  start_time   <     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     25     HOUR  )  )     OVER     (  )  ,     3  )     AS   baseline_share  ,
round  (  countIf  (  start_time   >=     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     25     HOUR  )
/     sum  (  countIf  (  start_time   >=     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     25     HOUR  )  )     OVER     (  )  ,     3  )     AS   recent_share  ,
round  (  recent_share   -   baseline_share  ,     3  )     AS   share_change
FROM   spans
WHERE   span_type   =     'TOOL'
AND   start_time   >=     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     193     HOUR
AND   trace_id   IN     (
SELECT   id   FROM   traces
WHERE   top_span_name   =     'research_agent'
AND   start_time   >=     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     193     HOUR
AND   start_time   <     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     1     HOUR
)
GROUP     BY   tool
ORDER     BY   abs  (  share_change  )     DESC


```


fetch_page


rose from 38.4% to 50.2% of tool calls, giving you a place to investigate. This requires the TOOL


[span type](https://laminar.sh/docs/tracing/structure/span-types) . Integrations set it; manual observe


wrappers must set it explicitly.


Next, measure three consecutive calls to the same tool:


```text
WITH   runs   AS     (
SELECT
trace_id  ,
if  (  min  (  start_time  )     >=     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     25     HOUR  ,     'recent'  ,     'baseline'  )     AS   window  ,
arrayMap  (  t   -  >   tupleElement  (  t  ,     2  )  ,   arraySort  (  groupArray  (  (  start_time  ,   name  )  )  )  )     AS   tools
FROM   spans
WHERE   span_type   =     'TOOL'
AND   start_time   >=     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     193     HOUR
AND   trace_id   IN     (
SELECT   id   FROM   traces
WHERE   top_span_name   =     'research_agent'
AND   start_time   >=     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     193     HOUR
AND   start_time   <     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     1     HOUR
)
GROUP     BY   trace_id
)
SELECT
window  ,
count  (  )     AS   runs  ,
round  (  avg  (  arrayExists  (  i   -  >   tools  [  i  ]     =   tools  [  i   +     1  ]     AND   tools  [  i  ]     =   tools  [  i   +     2  ]  ,
range  (  1  ,   greatest  (  length  (  tools  )     -     1  ,     1  )  )  )  )  ,     3  )     AS   same_tool_3x_rate
FROM   runs
GROUP     BY   window


```


The query orders tool calls by start time and only sees runs with tool spans. Both tool queries split the windows on span timestamps, so a run that crosses the 25-hour boundary can fall in a different window than in the main query.


The repeated-call rate rose from 39.7% to 61.5%. Fetching three pages consecutively is normal for this agent: a fixed three-call alert would fire on about 40% of baseline runs. For an obvious single-run loop, such as identical arguments twenty times, use a Signal to inspect arguments; this query doesn't.


## Outcome drift: failure share and new failure modes#


Track both increasing finding rates and potentially new failure modes.


For the first, measure the share of analyzed runs with an Issues finding. The Issues[Signal](https://laminar.sh/docs/signals/introduction) is preselected for new projects. For a daily trend, reuse the check's analyzed


and flagged


subqueries on traces


, group by toStartOfDay(start_time)


, and chart the share on a[dashboard](https://laminar.sh/docs/platform/dashboards) .


Laminar groups Signal events into[clusters](https://laminar.sh/docs/signals/clusters) by the meaning of their findings. A **New cluster**[alert](https://laminar.sh/docs/signals/alerts) fires when a cluster appears. UI-created Signals start with this alert, but it requires the clustering service and stays silent on deployments without it.


Scheduled[reports](https://laminar.sh/docs/signals/reports) compare event counts with the previous period and rank clusters by change. Those counts aren't traffic-normalized. Reports identify growing finding groups; SQL measures the affected share of analyzed runs.


## Attribute the shift before calling it a regression#


Both agents moved. Group metrics by possible explanations: release, model and input segment.


```text
SELECT
top_span_name   AS   agent  ,
release  ,
simpleJSONExtractString  (  metadata  ,     'source'  )     AS   source  ,
if  (  start_time   >=     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     25     HOUR  ,     'recent'  ,     'baseline'  )     AS   window  ,
count  (  )     AS   runs  ,
round  (  runs   /     sum  (  runs  )     OVER     (  PARTITION     BY   agent  ,   window  )  ,     3  )     AS   share_of_window  ,
round  (  avg  (  total_tokens  )  )     AS   avg_tokens
FROM   traces
WHERE   start_time   >=     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     193     HOUR
AND   start_time   <     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     1     HOUR
GROUP     BY   agent  ,     release  ,   source  ,   window
ORDER     BY   agent  ,     release  ,   source  ,   window


```


agent release source window runs share avg tokens


research_agent a1c93e0 baseline 2,494 0.97 49,926


research_agent 7d2f41b baseline 71 0.03 72,394


research_agent 7d2f41b recent 441 1.00 71,836


ticket_triage e40b7aa chat baseline 761 0.82 1,482


ticket_triage e40b7aa chat recent 74 0.46 1,404


ticket_triage e40b7aa email baseline 172 0.18 15,370


ticket_triage e40b7aa email recent 87 0.54 15,523


**The research agent's shift points to the release.** The 71 baseline runs on 7d2f41b


include the canary and the first hours of full rollout. In the 12-hour canary alone, 46 runs on 7d2f41b


averaged 76,699 tokens against 49,695 for 130 runs on a1c93e0


during the same hours. Concurrent canaries strengthen attribution when the router assigns runs independently of input. This still isn't proof: inspect the release diff next.


**The triage agent's shift looks like input drift.** It used one release throughout. Tokens per run barely moved within each source, while email tickets, ten times longer, rose from 18% to 54% of runs. You may need more capacity or an email-specific prompt, but a rollback is unlikely to change the traffic mix.


Record these attribution fields:


- **Release.** Set a release explicitly or use LMNR_RELEASE


; automatic detection also checks platform variables and .git


. The recorded value is available as traces.release


.
- **Model.** spans.model


contains the response model, falling back to the request model. The simulation's model changed a week before the shift, which argues against an immediate model-switch explanation.
- **Input segment.** Group a[trace metadata](https://laminar.sh/docs/tracing/metadata) key using simpleJSONExtractString(metadata, '<key>')


. Without segments, task-mix changes and regressions can produce the same aggregate shift.


[Agent versions](https://laminar.sh/docs/tracing/agent-versions) (beta) adds a fourth dimension: traces.agent_versions


records versions of system prompts and tool definitions. Use ARRAY JOIN agent_versions AS v


and group by v.version_hash


to align prompt or tool changes with the shift.


## Run the drift check on a schedule#


Laminar's native alerts cover Signal events and new clusters, not metric thresholds. Run your baseline query through the[SQL API](https://laminar.sh/docs/platform/sql-editor#sql-api) . Save it as drift_check.sql


and schedule this script with cron.


At each check, it reports run-shape changes and unavailable outcome statistics. Issues-share alerts require two consecutive threshold crossings:


```text
import   json
import   os
import   urllib  .  request
from   pathlib   import   Path


from   lmnr   import   LaminarClient


TOOLS_Z   =     4
FLAGGED_Z   =     3
STATE   =   Path  (  "drift_state.json"  )


client   =   LaminarClient  (  )
rows   =   client  .  sql  .  query  (  Path  (  "drift_check.sql"  )  .  read_text  (  )  )
previous   =   json  .  loads  (  STATE  .  read_text  (  )  )     if   STATE  .  exists  (  )     else     {  }
current   =     {  }
messages   =     [  ]


for   r   in   rows  :
agent   =   r  [  "agent"  ]
if   r  [  "tools_z"  ]     is     not     None     and     abs  (  r  [  "tools_z"  ]  )     >=   TOOLS_Z  :
messages  .  append  (
f"*  {  agent  }  * tool calls/run   {  r  [  'baseline_tools'  ]  }   ->   {  r  [  'recent_tools'  ]  }   "
f"(z=  {  r  [  'tools_z'  ]  }  ), tokens   {  r  [  'tokens_change'  ]  :  +.0%  }  "
)
if   r  [  "flagged_z"  ]     is     None  :
messages  .  append  (
f"*  {  agent  }  * Issues share unavailable:   {  r  [  'recent_analyzed'  ]  }   analyzed runs, "
f"coverage   {  r  [  'recent_coverage'  ]  }  "
)
elif   r  [  "flagged_z"  ]     >=   FLAGGED_Z  :
current  [  agent  ]     =     True
if   previous  .  get  (  agent  )  :
messages  .  append  (
f"*  {  agent  }  * Issues share   {  r  [  'baseline_flagged'  ]  }   ->   {  r  [  'recent_flagged'  ]  }   "
f"(z=  {  r  [  'flagged_z'  ]  }  ) on two consecutive checks"
)


STATE  .  write_text  (  json  .  dumps  (  current  )  )


for   text   in   messages  :
print  (  text  )
if   url   :=   os  .  environ  .  get  (  "SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL"  )  :
req   =   urllib  .  request  .  Request  (
url  ,
data  =  json  .  dumps  (  {  "text"  :   text  }  )  .  encode  (  )  ,
headers  =  {  "Content-Type"  :     "application/json"  }  ,
)
urllib  .  request  .  urlopen  (  req  )


```


LaminarClient


reads LMNR_PROJECT_API_KEY


. Persist drift_state.json


between checks and avoid concurrent jobs overwriting it. Overlapping windows share most runs, so confirmation filters one-off spikes without doubling statistical evidence.


This is scheduled screening, not immediate loop detection. Realtime-mode Signals return results in minutes; batch-mode results arrive within several hours. Choose the maturity lag accordingly.


## AI agent drift detection tools compared#


Products differ in what they baseline and how you configure alerts:


- **Datadog Agent Observability** emits ml_obs.*


metrics for traces, errors, durations and tokens. Its metrics documentation says they work in monitors like other metrics, so anomaly monitors can baseline them without SQL. Patterns clusters traffic into topics and shows change since the previous run.
- **Arize AX** monitors tracing projects on span attributes, including latency, status, token counts, eval labels and custom metadata. It offers automatic thresholds based on historical data. Separately, its ML-monitoring documentation covers baseline drift metrics such as PSI, KL, JS and embedding distance.
- **Evidently** detects text drift by training a classifier to distinguish reference and current data. WhyLabs' **whylogs** supports input-feature drift detection. Evidently's FAQ says its Cloud is no longer offered as SaaS. WhyLabs says it is discontinuing operations; its platform has been open-sourced.
- **Braintrust** clusters logs into Topics and alerts when a SQL calculation over a time window crosses a threshold you set.
- **LangSmith** offers threshold alerts for run count, errors, latency, cost and feedback scores. Insights analyzes usage patterns, behaviors and failure modes. **Langfuse** offers threshold-based alerts.


An embedding-based input-drift monitor fits semantic topic changes better than these tool-count queries, especially when new requests still use the same tools.


What Laminar contributes here is the shared SQL surface for per-run, per-tool and per-Signal data, followed by release and segment attribution. It also analyzes traces for failures and alerts on new finding clusters. Choose it for that workflow, not because it learns metric baselines automatically.


## FAQ#


### How many runs do I need before a drift check means anything?#


Enough that noise is smaller than the change you care about. At a pooled finding share near 6%, with 2,500 baseline and 400 recent analyzed runs, the standard error is about 1.3 percentage points. A difference of about 3.8 points reaches a z of 3. With fewer analyzed runs, compare weeks instead of days.


### Why compare against the previous 7 days instead of yesterday?#


A 7-day baseline averages weekday and weekend traffic, which can differ in task mix and volume. Day-over-day comparisons can flag predictable Monday changes. With a strong weekly pattern, compare against the same weekday in prior weeks instead.


### Will a provider changing the model behind an alias show up?#


The model field can expose the switch if the provider returns a distinct snapshot name. If the response repeats the alias, spans.model


won't reveal it; a behavioral shift alone cannot identify a model change. Query min(start_time)


per model to find each visible identifier's first appearance. The[Agent versions docs](https://laminar.sh/docs/tracing/agent-versions) explain why models are tracked separately from prompt versions.
